name: Japanese horse mackerel

cooks.name: Sashimi and namero (chopped with miso)
cooks.desc: Best raw when very fresh. Namero is chopped with miso and herbs, a dish from the Boso coast.

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: Salt it, rest briefly, pat dry, then grill so the flesh firms up.

cooks.name: Fried and nanban-zuke (fried then marinated in vinegar)
cooks.desc: Butterfly and deep-fry. Nanban-zuke keeps well and is good cold.

cooks.name: Himono (dried and grilled)
cooks.desc: Split along the back, brine, then dry overnight to concentrate the flavour.

pick: Look for clear, domed eyes and bright red gills. The body should feel firm, with well-formed scutes (the row of spiny scales near the tail).
keep: Best eaten the day you buy it. To keep, remove gills and guts, pat dry, wrap and chill. From the next day on, cook rather than eat raw.
trivia: Available year-round, but richest just before spawning in early summer. Fish that stay in one bay rather than migrating are called sezuki-aji; they are yellower and prized.

name: Japanese sardine

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Open by hand if fresh enough. Good with ginger and soy sauce.

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: When the fat is up, salt alone is enough.

cooks.name: Simmered with pickled ume
cooks.desc: Simmered with pickled ume until even the small bones soften.

cooks.name: Fish ball soup
cooks.desc: Chopped into balls and served in miso broth.

pick: Clear black spots along the flank and a blue sheen. The belly should be firm and the eyes not cloudy.
keep: Spoils quickly, so eat the same day. To keep, remove the head and guts, salt, and refrigerate.
trivia: Sardines caught during the rainy season are called nyubai-iwashi and are considered the fattest of the year.

name: Pacific saury

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: Grill over high heat at a distance. Connoisseurs eat the bitter innards too.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Only for very fresh fish. Good with ginger or garlic soy sauce.

cooks.name: Kabayaki and fish balls
cooks.desc: Filleted and glazed; the bones go into fish-ball soup.

pick: A faintly yellow snout and a dark blue sheen on the back. A firm belly, and the head should not droop when held.
keep: Spoils quickly, so eat the same day. Remove the guts before freezing.
trivia: Once a cheap everyday fish, poor catches in recent years have pushed prices up. Changing migration routes and rising sea temperatures are blamed.

name: Chub mackerel

cooks.name: Shime-saba (vinegar-cured mackerel)
cooks.desc: Cured in salt then vinegar. Freeze once first if eating raw.

cooks.name: Simmered in miso with ginger
cooks.desc: Simmered in miso with plenty of ginger. A household staple.

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: Served with grated daikon.

cooks.name: Tatsuta-age (marinated, starch-coated and fried)
cooks.desc: Marinating before frying softens the smell.

pick: Crisp markings on the back and a silvery-white belly. Firm flesh, and a rounded body means plenty of fat.
keep: Loses freshness especially fast; process it the same day. Freeze once before eating raw.
trivia: Richest from autumn into winter, known then as aki-saba and kan-saba. Branded lines such as Seki-saba and Matsuwa-saba are well known.

name: Japanese amberjack

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Winter buri is rich with fat.

cooks.name: Buri daikon (yellowtail simmered with daikon)
cooks.desc: Using the head and bones gives a better broth.

cooks.name: Teriyaki
cooks.desc: Glazed with a sweet-savoury sauce.

cooks.name: Buri shabu
cooks.desc: Thin slices swished briefly; the fat renders and it eats lighter.

pick: A bright red bloodline and firm flesh. In fillets, look for white fat marbled evenly through.
keep: Pat fillets dry, wrap and refrigerate. Sashimi-grade should be eaten the same day.
trivia: A fish that changes name as it grows. In Kansai: tsubasu, hamachi, mejiro, buri. In Kanto: wakashi, inada, warasa, buri.

name: Skipjack tuna

cooks.name: Tataki (seared outside, sliced)
cooks.desc: Seared then chilled. Served with garlic, ginger and onion.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Autumn returning bonito is rich and full-flavoured.

cooks.name: Kakuni (cubes simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Simmered with ginger in sweet soy. Keeps well.

cooks.name: Namaribushi (lightly steamed and dried loin)
cooks.desc: Steamed and lightly dried. Good in salads and dressed dishes.

pick: In fillets, the bloodline should be vivid and the flesh translucent. It darkens as time passes.
keep: Discolours quickly, so eat the same day. Wrap fillets tightly against the flesh and refrigerate.
trivia: Spring hatsu-gatsuo is lean and clean; autumn modori-gatsuo is rich with fat. The same fish tastes very different.

name: Pacific bluefin tuna

cooks.name: Sashimi and sushi
cooks.desc: Each cut tastes different: lean akami, medium chutoro, fatty otoro.

cooks.name: Zuke (marinated in soy sauce)
cooks.desc: Marinated in soy sauce. Suits the lean akami.

cooks.name: Negima nabe (tuna and leek hot pot)
cooks.desc: Chunks simmered with leek. An old Edo dish.

cooks.name: Grilled fish collar
cooks.desc: Salted and grilled. The meat near the bone is the best part.

pick: Akami should be vivid with fine, even grain. Toro should show parallel lines of fat.
keep: Eat the same day when refrigerated. If freezing, freeze fast and thaw only what you will eat.
trivia: Pole-and-line fishing at Oma in Aomori is famous. Full-cycle aquaculture is now established, easing pressure on wild stocks.

name: Red seabream

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Delicate and refined. Curing with kelp deepens the flavour.

cooks.name: Tai-meshi (sea bream rice)
cooks.desc: Fillets cooked together with rice.

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: A fixture at celebrations.

cooks.name: Ara-daki (head and bones simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Head and collar simmered in sweet soy.

pick: Clear eyes and a vivid pink body. The tail fin should not be darkened; wild fish have pointed tail tips.
keep: Keeps relatively well. Gutted and refrigerated, it lasts two to three days.
trivia: Before spawning in spring the body takes on a cherry-blossom pink and it is called sakura-dai. It features at celebrations for its colour, shape and keeping quality.

name: Olive flounder

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Sliced paper-thin. The engawa muscle along the fin is especially rich.

cooks.name: Kobujime (cured between kelp sheets)
cooks.desc: Cured overnight with kelp to concentrate the flavour.

cooks.name: Meunière
cooks.desc: Pan-fried in butter, which suits the delicate flesh.

cooks.name: Nitsuke (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Simmered in sweet soy.

pick: Thick flesh with a clean white underside, and springy to the touch.
keep: Fillet, pat dry, wrap and refrigerate. Use within one or two days.
trivia: Winter fish are called kan-hirame, firm and full of flavour. A saying goes that hirame faces left and karei faces right.

name: Marbled flounder

cooks.name: Nitsuke (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: The classic. Simmered in sweet soy with ginger.

cooks.name: Karaage (marinated and deep-fried)
cooks.desc: Small ones are fried whole, bones and all.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Good raw when fresh. The engawa is the prize.

cooks.name: Himono (dried and grilled)
cooks.desc: Dried overnight and grilled.

pick: Thick flesh with a white underside, a slippery coating and clear eyes.
keep: Gut and refrigerate. Use within one or two days.
trivia: Joka-karei from Hiji in Oita grows where fresh water wells up, and is known for having no muddy taste.

name: Chum salmon

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: The standard. Grilled until the skin is fragrant.

cooks.name: Chanchan-yaki (griddled with miso and vegetables)
cooks.desc: Griddled with vegetables and miso. A Hokkaido speciality.

cooks.name: Meunière
cooks.desc: Pan-fried in butter with lemon.

cooks.name: Ishikari nabe (salmon and vegetable miso hot pot)
cooks.desc: Head, bones and vegetables simmered in miso broth.

pick: Deep, even flesh colour with fine white marbling. Fillet edges should not be ragged.
keep: Pat fillets dry, wrap and refrigerate. Freezes well and is easy to handle.
trivia: Fat fish caught just before returning to the rivers are called tokishirazu or keiji, and are treated as rarities.

name: Japanese Spanish mackerel

cooks.name: Saikyo-yaki (marinated in sweet miso, grilled)
cooks.desc: Marinated in sweet white miso and grilled; the miso suits the mild flesh.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Good raw when fresh. Popular in the Kansai region.

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: The flesh is soft, so handle it carefully.

cooks.name: Tatsuta-age (marinated, starch-coated and fried)
cooks.desc: Marinated, then deep-fried.

pick: A silver sheen and firm flesh. Fillets should be white and translucent.
keep: The flesh is soft and breaks easily. Wrap and refrigerate, using within one or two days.
trivia: The kanji combines fish and spring, yet in Kanto the winter kan-zawara is preferred. The season is understood differently by region.

name: Largehead hairtail

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: Grill the skin side until fragrant. Simple is best.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Good raw when fresh, or lightly seared with the skin on.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: The flesh turns light and fluffy.

cooks.name: Nitsuke (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Simmered in sweet soy.

pick: The silver skin should be intact and glossy. The wider the body, the more fat.
keep: The silver skin comes off easily, so handle gently. Refrigerate for one or two days.
trivia: The silver coating is guanine, once used to make imitation pearls.

name: Whitespotted conger

cooks.name: Simmered conger eel
cooks.desc: Simmered in a sweet glaze until tender. A sushi favourite.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Light batter, fried until crisp.

cooks.name: Shirayaki (grilled plain, no sauce)
cooks.desc: Grilled plain with salt and wasabi to taste the fish itself.

cooks.name: Anago-meshi (conger eel over rice)
cooks.desc: Glazed and served over rice in a lacquer box.

pick: A slippery surface, a white belly and clear eyes.
keep: Spoils quickly; process the same day. Once split, refrigerate for one day.
trivia: Akashi in Hyogo and Tokyo Bay are known sources. Leaner than freshwater eel, so the flavour is lighter.

name: Splendid alfonsino

cooks.name: Nitsuke (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: The classic. Simmered in sweet soy until the flesh flakes.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Rich with fat and noticeably sweet.

cooks.name: Shabu-shabu
cooks.desc: Thin slices swished briefly in hot broth.

cooks.name: Himono (dried and grilled)
cooks.desc: Dried overnight and grilled.

pick: A vivid orange-red body, large clear eyes and intact scales.
keep: Gut and refrigerate; keeps two to three days.
trivia: Shimoda in Shizuoka and Choshi in Chiba are the main ports. It lives at 200 to 800 metres; the large eyes are an adaptation to the dark.

name: Sweetfish

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: Skewered to look as if swimming. The bitter innards are part of it.

cooks.name: Segoshi (sliced crosswise through the bone)
cooks.desc: Small fish sliced crosswise through the bone.

cooks.name: Kanroni (simmered in sweet soy syrup)
cooks.desc: Simmered slowly until the bones soften.

cooks.name: Uruka (salted fermented sweetfish innards)
cooks.desc: Salted innards. A drinker's delicacy.

pick: A firm body with clear yellow spots and a good aroma.
keep: Spoils quickly, so eat the same day. Gut before freezing.
trivia: Also written as the fragrant fish; the scent comes from the river algae it eats. Roe-bearing fish moving downstream are called ochi-ayu and are prized.

name: Chicken grunt

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Rich and sweet. Also good with the skin lightly seared.

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: The flesh turns light and fluffy.

cooks.name: Nitsuke (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Simmered in sweet soy.

cooks.name: Acqua pazza
cooks.desc: Also suits Western-style poaching.

pick: A yellowish body, good thickness and clear eyes.
keep: Gut and refrigerate. Use within one or two days.
trivia: Fattest during the rainy season, when it is called tsuyu-isaki. Young fish have yellow stripes and are nicknamed uribo.

name: Japanese barracuda

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: Watery flesh, so salt it more generously.

cooks.name: Himono (dried and grilled)
cooks.desc: Drying overnight concentrates the flavour.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Good raw when fresh, or with the skin seared.

cooks.name: Panko-breaded and deep-fried
cooks.desc: The mild flesh suits deep-frying.

pick: A silver sheen, a firm pointed snout and a taut body.
keep: High water content makes it spoil easily. Salt and refrigerate, or dry it.
trivia: A saying holds that grilled kamasu makes you eat a whole measure of rice.

name: Atka mackerel

cooks.name: Butterflied and dried
cooks.desc: The standard. Grilled and served with grated daikon.

cooks.name: Chanchan-yaki (griddled with miso and vegetables)
cooks.desc: Griddled with vegetables and miso.

cooks.name: Panko-breaded and deep-fried
cooks.desc: The mild flesh works well.

cooks.name: Tsumire (hand-formed fish balls)
cooks.desc: Chopped into balls for soup.

pick: For dried fish, thick flesh that is not over-dried. Fresh fish should have clear eyes and a firm body.
keep: Fresh fish spoils extremely fast; eat the same day. Dried fish freezes well.
trivia: Because it spoils so fast, it is sold almost only dried outside the producing region. Rausu in Hokkaido is well known.

name: Threadsail filefish

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Dipping in soy sauce mixed with the liver is the connoisseur's way.

cooks.name: Sashimi dressed with the liver
cooks.desc: Sashimi dressed with the liver. Very rich.

cooks.name: Nitsuke (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Simmered in sweet soy.

cooks.name: Nabe (hot pot)
cooks.desc: The mild flesh soaks up the broth.

pick: A large, swollen liver, a firm body and clear eyes.
keep: Skin, gut and refrigerate. Keep the liver separately and use it quickly.
trivia: The name comes from how easily the skin peels off. In winter the liver fattens, earning it the nickname sea foie gras.

name: Tiger pufferfish

cooks.name: Tessa (paper-thin pufferfish sashimi)
cooks.desc: Sliced thin enough to see the plate pattern through it.

cooks.name: Tecchiri (pufferfish hot pot)
cooks.desc: Made into hot pot. The bones give an excellent broth.

cooks.name: Karaage (marinated and deep-fried)
cooks.desc: Marinated, then deep-fried.

cooks.name: Hirezake (warm sake with toasted fin)
cooks.desc: A toasted fin steeped in hot sake.

pick: Translucent, springy flesh. Buy it already processed.
keep: Refrigerate for one or two days. Thin-sliced sashimi should be eaten the same day.
trivia: Preparation requires a specific licence. Shimonoseki in Yamaguchi is the trading centre. Preparing it without a licence is illegal.

name: Monkfish

cooks.name: Anko nabe (monkfish hot pot)
cooks.desc: The classic. Dissolving the liver into the miso broth makes it very rich.

cooks.name: Ankimo (steamed monkfish liver)
cooks.desc: Steamed and served with ponzu.

cooks.name: Karaage (marinated and deep-fried)
cooks.desc: The flesh is marinated and deep-fried.

cooks.name: Dressed with vinegared miso from the same fish
cooks.desc: Skin and flesh dressed with vinegared miso.

pick: Translucent flesh with a slippery coating. The liver should be white and firm.
keep: Separate the parts and refrigerate. Use within one or two days.
trivia: A saying pairs pufferfish in the west with monkfish in the east. Almost everything but the bones is eaten, divided into what are called the seven tools.

name: Pacific cod

cooks.name: Nabe (hot pot)
cooks.desc: The mild flesh soaks up the broth. The milt goes in too.

cooks.name: Meunière
cooks.desc: Pan-fried in butter.

cooks.name: Panko-breaded and deep-fried
cooks.desc: The flesh turns light and fluffy.

cooks.name: Tara-chiri (cod in kelp broth with ponzu)
cooks.desc: Simmered briefly in kelp broth and dipped in ponzu.

pick: White, translucent flesh with some spring to it. Fillets should not be ragged.
keep: High water content makes it spoil easily. Salting to draw out water before cooking helps.
trivia: The winter milt is called tachiko or kikuko and is prized. The Japanese word for eating your fill is said to derive from this fish.

name: Whitebait

cooks.name: Raw whitebait
cooks.desc: Only available at the source. Served with ginger and soy sauce.

cooks.name: Kamaage shirasu (boiled whitebait)
cooks.desc: Boiled. Served straight over rice.

cooks.name: Dried whitebait
cooks.desc: Lightly dried, so it keeps longer.

cooks.name: Kakiage (mixed tempura fritter)
cooks.desc: Fried together with chopped spring onion.

pick: Evenly sized and translucent. Raw shirasu must be landed the same day.
keep: Raw shirasu must be eaten the same day. Boiled keeps two to three days refrigerated, and freezes.
trivia: A collective name for juvenile sardines. Suruga Bay in Shizuoka and the Shonan coast in Kanagawa are known sources.

name: Japanese common squid

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Cut into fine strips. Also good dressed with the innards.

cooks.name: Grilled whole squid
cooks.desc: Grilled whole and brushed with soy sauce.

cooks.name: Shiokara (salt-fermented seafood)
cooks.desc: The flesh cured with its own innards.

cooks.name: Nitsuke (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Simmered with taro or daikon.

pick: A translucent, reddish-brown body; it turns cloudy white with time. The eyes should be clear.
keep: Remove the innards and refrigerate. Sashimi-grade should be eaten the same day. Freezes well.
trivia: The most widely eaten squid in Japan. Poor catches in recent years have pushed prices up.

name: Spear squid

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Sweet and tender.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: The tender flesh suits deep-frying.

cooks.name: Nitsuke (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Simmer briefly; overcooking turns it rubbery.

cooks.name: Grilled
cooks.desc: Grilled whole.

pick: A slim, translucent body. The flesh should not be cloudy.
keep: Remove the innards and refrigerate. Sashimi-grade should be eaten the same day.
trivia: Thinner and more tender than surume-ika. The name comes from its spear-like shape.

name: Common octopus

cooks.name: Boiled octopus
cooks.desc: Rub with salt before boiling. Used for sashimi or vinegared dishes.

cooks.name: Octopus rice
cooks.desc: Cooked together with rice.

cooks.name: Karaage (marinated and deep-fried)
cooks.desc: Marinated, then deep-fried.

cooks.name: Slow-simmered until tender
cooks.desc: Simmering with daikon helps tenderise it.

pick: Large, evenly sized suckers. Fresh octopus should be firm and deeply coloured.
keep: Boiled octopus keeps two to three days refrigerated, and freezes well.
trivia: Akashi in Hyogo is especially known. Strong currents give the octopus thick legs and firm flesh.

name: Kuruma prawn

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: Grilled in the shell. Very fragrant.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Straightened out, then fried.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Eaten live as odorigui.

cooks.name: Umani (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Simmered in sweet soy.

pick: Taut shells with clear markings. Live prawns are best.
keep: Keep live prawns in sawdust in the fridge. Cooked prawns keep one or two days.
trivia: The name comes from the wheel-like pattern when it curls up. Wild stocks have declined and most are now farmed.

name: Snow crab

cooks.name: Whole boiled crab
cooks.desc: Boiled in salted water and eaten as is.

cooks.name: Grilled crab legs
cooks.desc: Grilled in the shell; the aroma is wonderful.

cooks.name: Kani-suki (crab hot pot)
cooks.desc: Made into hot pot, finished with rice porridge.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Live crab chilled in ice water so the meat blooms.

pick: Heavy for its size, with a hard shell and all legs intact.
keep: Boiled crab keeps two to three days refrigerated. Cook raw crab the same day.
trivia: Each region has its own brand name: Echizen-gani in Fukui, Taiza-gani in Kyoto, Matsuba-gani in the San'in area. The season runs from early November to late March.

name: Horsehair crab

cooks.name: Whole boiled crab
cooks.desc: Boiled in salted water. The crab innards are very rich.

cooks.name: Crab innards warmed in the shell
cooks.desc: Warmed in the shell. A drinker's favourite.

cooks.name: Crab rice
cooks.desc: Picked meat cooked with rice.

cooks.name: Nabe (hot pot)
cooks.desc: Gives an excellent broth.

pick: Heavy for its size, with a hard shell and dense hair.
keep: Boiled crab keeps two to three days refrigerated.
trivia: Seasons differ around Hokkaido, so it is available almost year-round as the source shifts. Known less for its meat than for its rich innards.

name: Pacific oyster

cooks.name: Raw oysters
cooks.desc: With lemon or ponzu. Use oysters sold for raw consumption.

cooks.name: Kaki fry (panko-fried oysters)
cooks.desc: Coated in panko and deep-fried.

cooks.name: Dote-nabe (oyster hot pot with miso rim)
cooks.desc: Miso spread around the pot rim. A Hiroshima speciality.

cooks.name: Preserved in oil
cooks.desc: Cooked and preserved in oil. Keeps well.

pick: Shucked oysters should be plump and glossy, a creamy white. Avoid shrunken ones.
keep: Raw-grade and cooking-grade are used differently. Even raw-grade should be eaten within one or two days.
trivia: Called the milk of the sea. The difference between raw and cooking grade is not freshness but the hygiene standard of the harvest waters.

name: Manila clam

cooks.name: Miso soup
cooks.desc: The classic. Gives an excellent broth.

cooks.name: Sakamushi (steamed with sake)
cooks.desc: Steamed with sake and butter.

cooks.name: Spaghetti vongole
cooks.desc: Made into pasta with garlic and chilli.

cooks.name: Fukagawa-meshi (clams in miso over rice)
cooks.desc: Simmered in miso and served over rice. An old Edo dish.

pick: Shells closed, or closing immediately when touched, with clear markings.
keep: Purge sand in about 3% salt water, the same as seawater. Fresh water kills them. Freezes well.
trivia: Always purge in salt water. Fresh water weakens the clams, so salt must be dissolved in.

name: Hard clam

cooks.name: Osuimono (clear dashi soup)
cooks.desc: A fixture at the Doll Festival. A refined broth.

cooks.name: Grilled hard clams
cooks.desc: Grilled in the shell.

cooks.name: Sakamushi (steamed with sake)
cooks.desc: Steamed briefly with sake.

cooks.name: Nabe (hot pot)
cooks.desc: Gives a deep broth.

pick: Thick, glossy shells, tightly closed.
keep: Purge sand in salt water before cooking. Keeps two to three days refrigerated.
trivia: Because each shell only fits its own pair, it symbolises a lasting marriage and appears at weddings and the Doll Festival.

name: Scallop

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Very sweet. The adductor muscle sliced thin.

cooks.name: Pan-fried in butter with soy sauce
cooks.desc: Grilled in the half shell with a splash of soy sauce.

cooks.name: Panko-breaded and deep-fried
cooks.desc: Coated in panko and deep-fried.

cooks.name: Takikomi gohan (rice cooked with ingredients)
cooks.desc: Gives an excellent broth.

pick: The adductor muscle should be translucent and springy. Live scallops should close when touched.
keep: The adductor keeps one or two days refrigerated. It freezes, but loses liquid on thawing.
trivia: Hokkaido and Aomori account for most national production. Seabed-sown and hanging-culture scallops are said to taste different.

name: Turban shell

cooks.name: Tsuboyaki (grilled in its own shell)
cooks.desc: Grilled in its own shell with a splash of soy sauce.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Firm and crunchy.

cooks.name: Takikomi gohan (rice cooked with ingredients)
cooks.desc: Chopped and cooked with rice.

cooks.name: Sakamushi (steamed with sake)
cooks.desc: Steamed briefly with sake.

pick: A tightly closed operculum, heavy for its size, and it retracts when touched.
keep: Keep alive in the fridge wrapped in damp newspaper. Use within two or three days.
trivia: Grown in rough open water it develops long horns; in calm bays the horns are short or absent. The environment shows in the shape.

name: Abalone

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Sliced thin. The liver is edible too.

cooks.name: Sakamushi (steamed with sake)
cooks.desc: Steaming makes it tender.

cooks.name: Steak
cooks.desc: Pan-seared in butter.

cooks.name: Mizugai (chilled abalone in salted water)
cooks.desc: Floated in ice water as a summer refreshment.

pick: Plump flesh that contracts strongly when touched, with a thick shell.
keep: Keep alive in the fridge wrapped in damp newspaper. Cooked abalone keeps one or two days.
trivia: Several kinds exist, including kuro-awabi, megai-awabi and madaka-awabi. Kuro-awabi is the most expensive.

name: Freshwater clam

cooks.name: Miso soup
cooks.desc: The classic. Gives a deep broth.

cooks.name: Sakamushi (steamed with sake)
cooks.desc: Steamed briefly with sake.

cooks.name: Shijimi clam soup
cooks.desc: Also good in a clear broth.

cooks.name: Tsukudani (simmered in soy and sugar)
cooks.desc: The meat simmered in sweet soy.

pick: Thick, glossy dark brown shells, tightly closed.
keep: Purge sand in weak salt water of about 1%. Freezing is said to increase the umami compounds.
trivia: Lake Shinji in Shimane is the largest source. Both the summer doyo-shijimi and the winter kan-shijimi are considered at their best.

name: Sea urchin

cooks.name: Fresh sea urchin roe
cooks.desc: Eaten as is, or on sushi and rice bowls.

cooks.name: Grilled sea urchin roe
cooks.desc: Lightly grilled to bring out the aroma.

cooks.name: Uni-don (sea urchin over rice)
cooks.desc: Heaped over warm rice.

cooks.name: Pasta
cooks.desc: Works well in a cream sauce.

pick: Well-defined, unbroken lobes with vivid colour and no wateriness.
keep: Spoils quickly; eat the same day. Tray-packed roe varies in taste depending on the firming agent used.
trivia: Bafun uni is rich and sweet; murasaki uni is lighter. The part eaten is the gonad.

name: Salmon roe

cooks.name: Marinated in soy sauce
cooks.desc: The classic. Marinated in sake and soy sauce.

cooks.name: Ikura-don (salmon roe over rice)
cooks.desc: Piled generously over rice.

cooks.name: Salt-cured
cooks.desc: Cured in salt alone, letting the flavour stand out.

cooks.name: Oyako-don (salmon and salmon roe over rice)
cooks.desc: Salmon and salmon roe served together.

pick: Evenly sized eggs that are taut and glossy. Avoid broken ones.
keep: Soy-marinated roe keeps three to four days refrigerated. Portion and freeze for longer.
trivia: Loose eggs are ikura; the whole egg sac is sujiko. The word comes from Russian for fish roe.

name: Sea pineapple

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Distinctive aroma and sweetness. With vinegared soy sauce.

cooks.name: Sunomono (vinegared dish)
cooks.desc: Dressed with cucumber.

cooks.name: Grilled sea pineapple
cooks.desc: Grilled in the shell.

cooks.name: Shiokara (salt-fermented seafood)
cooks.desc: A pungent delicacy.

pick: Well-formed bumps on the surface, a firm body and a vivid orange colour.
keep: Spoils quickly and turns bitter with time; eat the same day.
trivia: Sanriku in Miyagi is the main source. Sometimes called the sea pineapple. Freshness makes a great difference to the taste.

name: Wakame seaweed

cooks.name: Miso soup
cooks.desc: The classic. Take care not to over-soak it.

cooks.name: Sunomono (vinegared dish)
cooks.desc: Dressed with cucumber.

cooks.name: Shabu-shabu
cooks.desc: Fresh wakame blanched briefly turns vivid green.

cooks.name: Mekabu (chopped wakame root)
cooks.desc: The root end pounded to bring out its stickiness.

pick: Fresh wakame should be deeply coloured and slippery. Dried wakame should be jet black and glossy.
keep: Salting fresh wakame makes it keep longer. Store dried wakame sealed at room temperature.
trivia: Sanriku and Naruto are the two great sources. Naruto wakame grows in fierce currents and has a notably firm bite.

name: Mozuku seaweed

cooks.name: Mozuku-su (seaweed in sweet vinegar)
cooks.desc: The classic. Dressed with sweetened vinegar.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Fried as a fritter; the texture changes completely.

cooks.name: Miso soup
cooks.desc: Added at the very end.

cooks.name: Soup
cooks.desc: Good in a Chinese-style egg drop soup.

pick: Evenly thick strands with a slippery coating and deep colour.
keep: Rinse the salt from salted mozuku first. Keeps two to three days refrigerated, and freezes.
trivia: Almost all mozuku sold in Japan comes from Okinawa. Okinawan mozuku is the thick-stranded type with a firm bite.

name: Nori seaweed

cooks.name: Toasted nori
cooks.desc: For rice balls and hand-rolled sushi.

cooks.name: Seasoned nori
cooks.desc: Brushed with a soy-based seasoning.

cooks.name: Tsukudani (simmered in soy and sugar)
cooks.desc: Fresh nori simmered in sweet soy.

cooks.name: Nori soup
cooks.desc: Floated in broth to enjoy the aroma.

pick: Deep black and glossy. Held to the light, it should be evenly translucent.
keep: Sensitive to humidity. Keep sealed with a desiccant and use quickly once opened.
trivia: The Ariake Sea in Saga is the largest source. The first winter harvest, ichiban-zumi, is the most tender and fragrant.

name: Greater amberjack

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Firmer than buri, with a more refined fat. Slice thin to bring out the bite.

cooks.name: Grilled collar
cooks.desc: Salted and grilled. The meat near the bone is the best part.

cooks.name: Teriyaki
cooks.desc: Glazed with a sweet-savoury sauce. The fillets are thick, so do not overcook.

cooks.name: Ara-daki (head and bones simmered)
cooks.desc: Head and collar simmered in sweet soy. Gives an excellent broth.

pick: Clear eyes and a firm body. Fillets should have a vivid bloodline and translucent pink flesh.
keep: Firmer flesh means it keeps better than buri. Pat fillets dry, wrap and refrigerate; use within about two days.
trivia: A diagonal dark band above the eye makes the head look like the kanji for eight when seen from the front, which is where the name comes from. It often fetches a higher price than buri.

name: Kichiji rockfish

cooks.name: Nitsuke (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Simmered in sweet soy. The rich fat suits a slightly stronger seasoning.

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: Grilled until the fat drips. The skin side turns fragrant.

cooks.name: Yubiki (skin briefly scalded)
cooks.desc: The skin is dipped in hot water and served as sashimi, bringing out its sweetness.

cooks.name: Dried overnight
cooks.desc: Brined and dried. The rich flavour concentrates.

pick: A vivid scarlet body with clear eyes. A firm belly and intact scales.
keep: Gut and refrigerate. The high fat content oxidises easily, so use within two days.
trivia: Its formal name is kichiji. Rausu kinki from Hokkaido is considered the finest. A deep-water fish with small catches, it is treated as a luxury.

name: Black scraper

cooks.name: Dressed with the liver
cooks.desc: Thin slices dressed with the liver, which is larger and richer than a filefish's.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Sliced thin and dipped in soy sauce mixed with the liver. The flesh is lean and firm.

cooks.name: Nabe (hot pot)
cooks.desc: The lean flesh soaks up the broth. The liver can be dissolved in as well.

cooks.name: Nitsuke (simmered in sweet soy)
cooks.desc: Simmered in sweet soy. The bones give a good broth.

pick: A large, swollen liver, a firm body and clear eyes.
keep: Skin, gut and refrigerate. Keep the liver separately and use it the same or the next day.
trivia: The long face resembling a horse gives it its name. Cheaper than kawahagi filefish but with a larger liver, so many choose it when the liver is the point.

name: Flying fish

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Lean and delicate. Good with ginger soy sauce or vinegared miso.

cooks.name: Shioyaki (salt-grilled)
cooks.desc: The flesh is firm. Grill the skin side until fragrant.

cooks.name: Tsumire (fish balls)
cooks.desc: Chopped into balls. Springy, and well suited to soups.

cooks.name: Yaki-ago (grilled and dried)
cooks.desc: Grilled then dried. In Kyushu it is essential for the broth of zoni and udon.

pick: A silver sheen with unbroken pectoral fins. Clear eyes and a firm belly.
keep: Loses freshness quickly; process the same day. Drying it allows long storage.
trivia: Called ago in Kyushu, where the grilled and dried fish makes a prized broth. It spreads its pectoral fins and glides several hundred metres over the sea.

name: Tilefish

cooks.name: Wakasa-yaki (grilled with scales on)
cooks.desc: Brushed with sake and grilled with the scales left on, so they stand up and crisp.

cooks.name: Sashimi
cooks.desc: Refined and sweet. Curing with kelp deepens the flavour.

cooks.name: In clear soup
cooks.desc: Delicate, refined flesh. In Kyoto cuisine it is the centrepiece of a clear soup.

cooks.name: Steamed
cooks.desc: Steamed with sake, or with grated turnip. The flesh turns light and fluffy.

pick: A pale pink body with clear eyes. A large, squared head and good thickness through the body.
keep: The flesh is soft and watery. Gut it, salt it lightly and refrigerate to firm it up. Use within two days.
trivia: Known as guji in Kyoto, where fish from Wakasa Bay are especially prized. Because they were lightly salted for the journey to Kyoto, the wakasa-yaki method was born.

name: Bamboo shoot

cooks.name: Wakatake-ni (bamboo shoot simmered with wakame)
cooks.desc: Simmered together with wakame. A spring staple, seasoned lightly so the dashi shows.

cooks.name: Bamboo shoot rice
cooks.desc: Tips sliced thin, base cut in cubes, for two textures.

cooks.name: Grilled bamboo shoot with kinome miso
cooks.desc: Freshly dug, grilled in the skin with kinome miso. Very little bitterness.

pick: Pale brown, moist skin with few, low bumps at the base. Green tips mean it has grown too far and will be bitter.
keep: Bitterness builds from the moment it is dug, so parboil the same day with rice bran and dried chilli. Once boiled, keep submerged in water in the fridge for four to five days.
trivia: Shirako bamboo shoots from Otokuni in Kyoto are grown under straw and mounded soil, which keeps them white and tender.

name: Asparagus

cooks.name: Boiled in salted water
cooks.desc: Peel the base of thick spears first. Good with mayonnaise or egg.

cooks.name: Grilled
cooks.desc: In a pan or on the grill; the sweetness deepens.

cooks.name: Wrapped in bacon
cooks.desc: A classic pairing.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Light batter, fried quickly.

pick: Tight, straight tips and a fresh-looking cut end. Thicker spears are more tender and sweeter.
keep: Refrigerate standing upright. Laid flat, the tips try to turn upward and the spears bend.
trivia: Grown without sunlight it becomes white asparagus. The same variety changes colour with the growing method.

name: New-crop onion

cooks.name: Thin-sliced onion salad
cooks.desc: Mild enough to eat raw. With bonito flakes and soy sauce.

cooks.name: Simmered whole
cooks.desc: Simmered whole in clear broth until soft.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Brings out the sweetness.

cooks.name: Onion soup
cooks.desc: Sweet even without browning first.

pick: Unblemished skin, heavy for its size, and a tight neck.
keep: High water content means it does not keep. About a week refrigerated; wrapping in newspaper helps.
trivia: Shipped straight after harvest, so it is juicy and mild. Ordinary onions are cured for about a month before shipping.

name: Cabbage

cooks.name: Finely shredded
cooks.desc: Spring cabbage is tender and suits eating raw.

cooks.name: Stuffed cabbage rolls
cooks.desc: Outer leaves blanched and rolled around a filling.

cooks.name: Hoikoro (stir-fried cabbage and pork with miso)
cooks.desc: For stir-frying. Winter cabbage stands up to heat.

cooks.name: Salted and squeezed
cooks.desc: Made into quick pickles.

pick: Spring cabbage should be loosely packed and light; winter cabbage firm and heavy. The cut end should not be discoloured.
keep: Cut out the core, pack the cavity with damp kitchen paper, bag it and refrigerate.
trivia: Spring cabbage is tender and suits raw dishes; winter cabbage has thick leaves for cooking. The same vegetable behaves differently by season.

name: Eggplant

cooks.name: Yaki-nasu (charred and peeled eggplant)
cooks.desc: Charred, peeled, and served with ginger and soy sauce.

cooks.name: Mabo nasu (eggplant in spicy bean sauce)
cooks.desc: Eggplant and oil go together well.

cooks.name: Age-bitashi (fried then steeped in dashi)
cooks.desc: Deep-fried plain, then steeped in dashi.

cooks.name: Tsukemono (Japanese pickles)
cooks.desc: Salted or bran-pickled.

pick: Taut, glossy skin with deep colour. Sharp thorns on the calyx mean it is fresh.
keep: Sensitive to cold. Wrap in newspaper and keep in the vegetable drawer. Below 5°C it deteriorates.
trivia: Many regional varieties exist: Kamo nasu in Kyoto, mizu nasu in Osaka, juzen nasu in Niigata, each different in shape and taste.

name: Cucumber

cooks.name: Sunomono (vinegared dish)
cooks.desc: Dressed with wakame or octopus.

cooks.name: Asazuke (lightly salted quick pickles)
cooks.desc: Rubbed with salt.

cooks.name: Smashed cucumber with sesame oil
cooks.desc: Smashed so the dressing soaks in.

cooks.name: Hiyashi chuka (chilled noodles)
cooks.desc: Cut into fine strips.

pick: Sharp bumps on the surface and an even thickness. It should feel hard and taut.
keep: Pat dry, bag, and refrigerate standing upright. Sensitive to cold, so do not over-chill.
trivia: About 95% water. Valued in summer as a food that cools the body.

name: Tomato

cooks.name: Salad
cooks.desc: Simply sliced, with salt and olive oil.

cooks.name: Tomato sauce
cooks.desc: Reduced to concentrate the umami.

cooks.name: Roasted tomatoes
cooks.desc: Heat brings out the sweetness.

cooks.name: Chilled pasta
cooks.desc: For summer.

pick: A green calyx that curls back, even colour all over, and heavy for its size.
keep: Ripen at room temperature before it is fully red, then refrigerate. Over-chilling dulls the flavour.
trivia: Heat makes the umami compound glutamate more available. Its role changes between raw and cooked dishes.

name: Green pepper

cooks.name: Stuffed with minced meat
cooks.desc: Halved and stuffed.

cooks.name: Stir-fried peppers and beef
cooks.desc: Cut into strips and stir-fried.

cooks.name: Whole grilled green peppers
cooks.desc: Grilled whole with soy sauce.

cooks.name: Kinpira (julienned and stir-fried)
cooks.desc: Stir-fried sweet and savoury.

pick: Glossy, taut skin with rounded shoulders, and a fresh-looking cut at the stem.
keep: Pat dry, bag and refrigerate. Keeps about a week.
trivia: Left to ripen it turns red, growing sweeter and less bitter. A different variety from bell peppers.

name: Kabocha squash

cooks.name: Nimono (simmered in dashi)
cooks.desc: Simmered in dashi and soy, sweet and savoury.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Sliced thin and fried.

cooks.name: Puréed soup
cooks.desc: Puréed with milk.

cooks.name: Gratin
cooks.desc: Works beautifully with cheese.

pick: A sunken area around the stem that is dry and cracked. Cut pieces should have packed seeds and deeply coloured flesh.
keep: Whole squash keeps one to two months in a well-ventilated room. Once cut, remove seeds and pith and refrigerate.
trivia: Stored one to two months after harvest, its starch turns to sugar and it sweetens. Harvested in summer, at its best in autumn.

name: Bitter melon

cooks.name: Goya champuru (stir-fried with tofu and egg)
cooks.desc: Stir-fried with tofu and egg. An Okinawan staple.

cooks.name: Tsukudani (simmered in soy and sugar)
cooks.desc: Simmered sweet and savoury.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Softens the bitterness.

cooks.name: Dressed vegetables
cooks.desc: Sliced thin, salted, then dressed.

pick: Dense, even bumps, deep colour, and firm to the touch.
keep: Remove seeds and pith, wrap and refrigerate. Once cut it spoils quickly.
trivia: The bitterness is concentrated in the seeds and pith. Salting or parboiling softens it. Ripe fruit turns yellow and loses its bitterness.

name: Okra

cooks.name: Ohitashi (blanched greens in dashi)
cooks.desc: Blanched briefly and steeped in dashi.

cooks.name: Chopped with natto
cooks.desc: Chopped with natto; the stickiness increases.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Fried whole.

cooks.name: Stir-fried
cooks.desc: Stir-fried with meat.

pick: Dense fine hairs and well-defined ridges. Oversized pods are tough.
keep: Sensitive to cold. Wrap in newspaper and keep in the vegetable drawer. Use within two or three days.
trivia: Rubbing the hairs off with salt improves the texture. Cutting before boiling lets the viscosity run out, so boil the pods whole.

name: Edamame

cooks.name: Boiled in salted water
cooks.desc: Boil in about 4% salted water. Don't overcook.

cooks.name: Pan-charred edamame
cooks.desc: Pan-charred in the pod. Very fragrant.

cooks.name: Zunda (mashed edamame with mochi)
cooks.desc: Mashed and served with mochi. A Tohoku speciality.

cooks.name: Kakiage (mixed tempura fritter)
cooks.desc: Beans shelled and fried as a fritter.

pick: Bright green pods with dense fine hairs and evenly swollen beans.
keep: Sugars start falling the moment it is picked. Boiling the same day is best; boiled beans freeze well.
trivia: Soybeans harvested before maturity. Heirloom varieties such as dadacha-mame in Yamagata and Kurosaki cha-mame in Niigata are well known.

name: Sweet corn

cooks.name: Boiled
cooks.desc: Boiling in the husk keeps it from going watery.

cooks.name: Grilled corn with soy sauce
cooks.desc: Brushed with soy sauce and grilled.

cooks.name: Kakiage (mixed tempura fritter)
cooks.desc: Kernels stripped and fried as a fritter.

cooks.name: Soup
cooks.desc: Puréed.

pick: Dense brown silk, deep green husks, and kernels packed right to the tip.
keep: Sugars start falling the moment it is picked. Cook the same day, or boil and refrigerate if not eating at once.
trivia: The number of silks equals the number of kernels. More silk means a better-filled ear.

name: Sweet potato

cooks.name: Yaki-imo (roasted sweet potato)
cooks.desc: Roasting slowly at low heat makes it sweeter.

cooks.name: Daigaku-imo (candied sweet potato)
cooks.desc: Fried and coated in syrup.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Sliced thin.

cooks.name: Steamed sweet potato
cooks.desc: Simply steamed to taste the potato itself.

pick: Deep, even skin colour with no cuts or hollows, and heavy in the hand.
keep: Sensitive to cold. Avoid the fridge; wrap in newspaper and keep somewhere cool and dark at room temperature.
trivia: Stored one to two months after harvest it grows sweeter. Heating slowly at low temperature lets enzymes work and sweetens it further.

name: Potato

cooks.name: Nikujaga (potato and beef simmered)
cooks.desc: Danshaku falls apart easily; May Queen holds its shape.

cooks.name: Potato salad
cooks.desc: The floury Danshaku variety suits it best.

cooks.name: French fries
cooks.desc: Soak in water before frying.

cooks.name: Steamed potato with butter
cooks.desc: Steamed or baked.

pick: Taut skin with no sprouts. Avoid any with a green tinge.
keep: Light turns them green, so store in the dark. Keeping them with an apple slows sprouting.
trivia: Green patches and sprouts contain solanine and must be removed thoroughly before cooking.

name: Taro

cooks.name: Nikkorogashi (simmered until glazed)
cooks.desc: Simmered sweet and savoury.

cooks.name: Imoni (taro and meat stew)
cooks.desc: Stewed with beef or pork. A Tohoku speciality.

cooks.name: Agedashi (fried and served in dashi)
cooks.desc: Deep-fried plain and served in dashi.

cooks.name: Miso soup
cooks.desc: Added to miso soup.

pick: Still soil-covered and moist, with clear banding, hard and firm.
keep: Sensitive to both cold and dryness. Leave the soil on, wrap in newspaper and keep somewhere cool and dark at room temperature.
trivia: The sliminess clouds simmering liquid, so it is usually removed by salting or parboiling, though it also carries umami.

name: Daikon radish

cooks.name: Oden (simmered assortment in dashi)
cooks.desc: Bevel the edges and parboil before simmering.

cooks.name: Buri daikon (yellowtail simmered with daikon)
cooks.desc: Simmered with fish so the flavour soaks in.

cooks.name: Grated daikon
cooks.desc: The tip end is the sharpest.

cooks.name: Kiriboshi daikon (dried daikon strips)
cooks.desc: Dried to keep longer.

pick: Heavy in the hand with taut skin. If the leaves are attached, they should look lively.
keep: Cut the leaves off before storing, or they draw moisture from the root. Wrap in newspaper and refrigerate.
trivia: The top is sweet and it grows sharper towards the tip. Use the top for salads and the tip for grating.

name: Carrot

cooks.name: Kinpira (julienned and stir-fried)
cooks.desc: Cut into strips and stir-fried.

cooks.name: Glazed with butter and sugar
cooks.desc: Glazed with butter and sugar.

cooks.name: Salad
cooks.desc: Cut into fine strips.

cooks.name: Puréed soup
cooks.desc: Puréed and strained.

pick: Deep colour with a glossy, smooth surface. A narrower core means more tender flesh.
keep: Pat dry, wrap in newspaper and refrigerate standing upright. Sensitive to humidity.
trivia: Beta-carotene is concentrated near the skin, and is absorbed better when eaten with oil.

name: Burdock root

cooks.name: Kinpira (julienned and stir-fried)
cooks.desc: The classic. Shaved thin and stir-fried.

cooks.name: Crushed burdock with sesame
cooks.desc: Crushed so the dressing soaks in.

cooks.name: Tonjiru (pork and vegetable miso soup)
cooks.desc: Added to pork soup for its aroma.

cooks.name: Karaage (marinated and deep-fried)
cooks.desc: Coated and deep-fried.

pick: Still soil-covered, without cracks, and even in thickness. Very thick roots can be hollow inside.
keep: Store with the soil on, wrapped in newspaper somewhere cool and dark. Washed roots dry out, so refrigerate them.
trivia: Rarely eaten outside Japan. The aroma sits near the skin, so scrape rather than peel.

name: Lotus root

cooks.name: Kinpira (julienned and stir-fried)
cooks.desc: Sliced thin and stir-fried.

cooks.name: Lotus root stuffed with minced meat and fried
cooks.desc: Sandwiched with minced meat and fried.

cooks.name: Su-basu (vinegared lotus root)
cooks.desc: Pickled in sweet vinegar.

cooks.name: Grated lotus root dumplings
cooks.desc: Grated into dumplings with a chewy texture.

pick: Evenly sized holes and a white cut face. Heavy, with no blemishes.
keep: Cover the cut face with film and refrigerate. It discolours in air; soaking in vinegared water keeps it white.
trivia: The tip end nearest the new shoot is tender, while the base end is stickier. Choose the part to suit the dish.

name: Napa cabbage

cooks.name: Nabe (hot pot)
cooks.desc: Soaks up the broth and turns sweet.

cooks.name: Tsukemono (Japanese pickles)
cooks.desc: Salt-pickled or made into kimchi.

cooks.name: Happosai (stir-fried vegetables in thick sauce)
cooks.desc: For stir-frying.

cooks.name: Simmered in cream sauce
cooks.desc: Heat brings out the sweetness.

pick: Heavy in the hand and tightly packed, with a fresh white cut face. Small black spots do not affect quality.
keep: Whole heads keep wrapped in newspaper standing upright somewhere cool and dark. Once cut it spoils from the cut face, so refrigerate.
trivia: Exposed to frost it stores sugar to avoid freezing, so the colder it gets the sweeter it becomes.

name: Spinach

cooks.name: Ohitashi (blanched greens in dashi)
cooks.desc: Blanched and steeped in dashi.

cooks.name: Goma-ae (dressed with ground sesame)
cooks.desc: Blanched and dressed with ground sesame.

cooks.name: Sautéed in butter
cooks.desc: Also good Western-style.

cooks.name: Miso soup
cooks.desc: Added at the very end.

pick: Thick, deep green leaves with a vivid red root end, and stems that are not too thick.
keep: Wrap in damp newspaper and refrigerate standing upright. Sensitive to drying.
trivia: The astringent compounds reduce when boiled and soaked in water. Winter spinach sweetens and is sold as chijimi horenso.

name: Komatsuna

cooks.name: Ohitashi (blanched greens in dashi)
cooks.desc: Low in bitterness, so no parboiling needed.

cooks.name: Stir-fried
cooks.desc: Stir-fried with fried tofu.

cooks.name: Miso soup
cooks.desc: Added to miso soup.

cooks.name: Smoothie
cooks.desc: Can be used raw.

pick: Thick, deeply coloured leaves with sturdy stems, not wilted.
keep: Wrap in damp newspaper and refrigerate standing upright. Use within two or three days.
trivia: Less astringent than spinach, so it can be used without parboiling. The name comes from the Komatsugawa area of Tokyo where it was grown.

name: Shungiku

cooks.name: Nabe (hot pot)
cooks.desc: For sukiyaki and hot pots.

cooks.name: Ohitashi (blanched greens in dashi)
cooks.desc: Blanched briefly.

cooks.name: Shira-ae (dressed with mashed tofu)
cooks.desc: Dressed with mashed tofu.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Brings out the aroma.

pick: Deep green leaves growing densely, a strong aroma, and slim tender stems.
keep: Wrap in damp newspaper and refrigerate. Sensitive to drying, and the aroma fades easily.
trivia: Known as kikuna in Kansai. Overcooking drives off the aroma, so add it last to a hot pot.

name: Naganegi leek

cooks.name: Charred grilled leek
cooks.desc: Grilled slowly until sweet.

cooks.name: Nabe (hot pot)
cooks.desc: Soaks up the broth and turns tender.

cooks.name: As a garnish
cooks.desc: Sliced into thin rings.

cooks.name: Nuta (dressed with vinegared miso)
cooks.desc: Dressed with vinegared miso.

pick: A long, firm white section with a clear boundary to the green, tightly wrapped.
keep: Wrap in newspaper and store upright somewhere cool and dark. Sliced leek should be sealed and refrigerated or frozen.
trivia: Kanto eats mainly the white part, Kansai mainly the green.

name: Myoga ginger

cooks.name: As a garnish
cooks.desc: Chopped over chilled tofu or somen.

cooks.name: Pickled in sweet vinegar
cooks.desc: Turns a vivid pink.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Fried whole.

cooks.name: Miso soup
cooks.desc: Added for its aroma.

pick: Plump and rounded with vivid colour, and tips not yet opening.
keep: Sensitive to drying. Wrap in damp kitchen paper, seal and refrigerate.
trivia: The part eaten is the flower bud. Kochi produces most of the national crop.

name: Shiso

cooks.name: As a garnish
cooks.desc: Chopped over sashimi or noodles.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Battered on one side only, then fried.

cooks.name: Wrapped in shiso and pan-fried
cooks.desc: Wrapped around meat or fish and grilled.

cooks.name: Juice
cooks.desc: Red shiso simmered into a cordial.

pick: Bright green leaves with a strong aroma, free of bruises and dark spots.
keep: Stand the stems in water and refrigerate, or wrap in damp paper and seal.
trivia: Green shiso is used as a garnish, red shiso for pickled plums and cordials. They are varieties of the same plant.

name: Broad bean

cooks.name: Boiled in salted water
cooks.desc: Shelled and boiled.

cooks.name: Broad beans grilled in the pod
cooks.desc: Grilled in the pod, which steams them.

cooks.name: Tempura
cooks.desc: Peel the thin inner skin first.

cooks.name: Green pea rice
cooks.desc: Folded into cooked rice.

pick: Taut, glossy pods still carrying fine hairs, with evenly swollen beans.

trivia: One of the few vegetables native to Japan. The flower bud that appears in early spring is fuki-no-to.

trivia: The gentle bitterness is the point. Once it flowers the astringency grows, so it is picked in bud.

trivia: In Miyagi the roots are eaten too, in seri nabe. The aroma and bite of the roots are what people value.

keep: Cut the leaves off and store them separately, or the root loses moisture.
trivia: The leaves are more nutritious than the root. Many heirloom varieties exist, such as Shogoin kabu in Kyoto and Hino-na kabu in Shiga.

keep: Do not wash. Wrap in damp newspaper and refrigerate. The aroma fades, so use quickly.
trivia: It cannot be cultivated, so only wild mushrooms exist. Japanese production has fallen sharply and most sold is imported.

trivia: Grown either on logs or on sawdust blocks. Drying increases both vitamin D and umami compounds.

trivia: The tip is sweeter than the stem end. Eating from the stem end keeps the last bite sweet.

trivia: The white pith under the skin is nutritious too. Sunny, well-drained slopes make the best growing land.
